extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulewriters, agency technical staff, environmental lawyers and advocacy groups preparing comments on CAA section 112 residual risk rulemakings
extracted.subtask_description: Public-interest legal/technical comments addressing EPA's obligations under Clean Air Act section 112(f)(2) and related provisions when conducting a residual risk assessment and proposing MACT/risk-based standards for oil and gas source categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reliable, measured emission test data
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA has offered no valid justification for not collecting and using reliable, measured emission test data in this rulemaking, when emissions information is the 'starting point' for the risk assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actual stack or emission point 'sampling' or testing is the preferred method for gathering a 'snapshot' of emission data from point sources: 'Samples are collected from the stack using probes inserted through a port in the stack wall, and pollutants are collected in or on various media and sent to a laboratory for analysis.' EPA should collect available state/industry test data (e.g., Texas) and may require testing under CAA section 114, 42 U.S.C. § 7414(a)(1), (c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for malfunctions, exceedances, and emissions during violations
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA has failed to account for the potential for malfunctions and exceedances of the standard; EPA’s estimates are not the 'actual' level of emissions for this source category including during periods of violation of the existing standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risk analyses and standards must consider emissions during malfunction or exceedance periods; the residual risk standard should be strengthened to account for likely underestimation of health risk due to such omissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventory must be demonstrably representative and rationally justified
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must provide a reasoned explanation of why its inventory is representative and why its choice of data is rational and consistent with the statutory requirement to provide an 'ample margin' to protect public health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The record must include evidence of the accuracy/completeness of the inventory; EPA must explain omissions and data choices so commenters can evaluate the risk assessment (important for informed comments under CAA section 307).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 112(f)(2) requires assessing all HAP emission points in the source category
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 112(f)(2) directs EPA to conduct a residual risk review for the entire source category (or subcategory), including all HAP emissions and emission points, not only those previously regulated under section 112(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promulgation of any section 112(d) standard for a source category triggers the obligation to conduct a complete section 112(f)(2) rulemaking for that entire category within 8 years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare MACT floor to emissions limitation that would eliminate adverse effects
rubrics_metrics.description: During the residual risk rulemaking EPA is required to compare the existing MACT limit with whatever emissions limitation would eliminate the adverse health and environmental effects caused by a source category; if the MACT allows emissions associated with adverse effects, EPA has a non-discretionary duty to impose further regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the Senate Report articulation: 'The Administrator is to compare the emissions limitation which would eliminate the adverse health and environmental effects ... If the technology standard allows emissions which may be associated with adverse effects, the Administrator has a non-discretionary duty to impose further regulation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not limit residual risk analysis to currently regulated emission points
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should not assess risk only from the 'currently regulated emission points' (those regulated by section 112(d)) because the existing MACT does not cover numerous other emission points in the sector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to assess uncontrolled and fugitive emission points likely underestimates health risk; EPA must assess and consider regulating uncontrolled points and fugitives as part of section 112(f)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess and consider specific emission points omitted from analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must assess risk from emission points such as storage vessels, equipment leaks, process vents (including amine treaters and sulfur recovery tail gas), pipeline pigging and wastes, combustion sources, storage/condensate tanks, wastewater impoundments, open-pit waste ponds, produced water, and well completion activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State and regional data (e.g., Colorado, Texas studies) indicate these are significant HAP sources (examples: condensate tanks >100 tpy VOCs in Colorado; well completion venting 1,000–24,000 mcf per well). EPA must evaluate these sources and consider proposing limits where warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revisit exemptions (black oil, throughput-based exclusions) and justify or eliminate them
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's re-promulgation of exemptions (e.g., 40 C.F.R. § 63.760(e) for black oil facilities and throughput exemptions) lacks assessment of associated health risks and is arbitrary when residual risk rulemaking is based on health considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the D.C. Circuit has recognized 'no control' MACT floors as unlawful, EPA must revisit exemptions and establish limits where required by health-based residual risk analysis (Sierra Club v. EPA cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat and regulate fugitive emissions broadly across the sector
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 112(n)(4) does not bar broad regulation of fugitive HAP emissions; EPA must consider fugitives broadly as a source of health risk and potential control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA may regulate piping and pneumatic valves and should ensure all valves/potential leak sources are regulated or explain exclusions; fugitives can include production equipment, drilling, completions, processing, transmission, and accumulated valve emissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA may and should revise the definition of 'associated equipment' to capture significant emitters
rubrics_metrics.description: To consider cumulative emissions from associated equipment, EPA can revise its 'associated equipment' definition to exclude emission points that emit HAPs in quantities comparable to other significant sources and thereby regulate them under the source category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA has previously excluded particular sources from 'associated equipment' consistent with congressional intent and practical criteria; it should do so again where appropriate to capture significant HAP contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include heavy metals and mercury in the emissions inventory and risk assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Emissions of cadmium, chromium, cobalt, lead, manganese, nickel, selenium, and mercury were removed from the inventory or not assessed; these metals have serious human and ecological health effects and must be evaluated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must justify any removal of metals from the inventory; given persistence and toxicity (e.g., lead neurotoxicity, methylmercury bioaccumulation), omitting metals likely underestimates risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include organic HAPs documented in field studies and ambient monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA omitted many organic HAPs documented by local studies (e.g., chloromethane, 1,3-butadiene, vinyl chloride, vinyl acetate, bromomethane, 1,1-dichloroethane, vinyl bromide, 1,3-dichloropropene, propylene dichloride, carbon tetrachloride; Sublette County list including several chlorinated compounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must investigate and include these HAPs in the residual risk assessment when studies and monitoring detect them near oil and gas facilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterize and assess HAPs from hydraulic fracturing chemicals and new drilling practices
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA appears to have failed to characterize the new and different types of HAP emissions that may occur due to hydraulic fracturing chemicals and modern drilling practices; many chemicals used are undisclosed or poorly characterized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA should consult disclosures (FracFocus), TDEX, the House Committee report listing at least 25 HAPs, and other sources to assess volatilization potential, quantities, and mixture effects (individual and cumulative) from fracturing-related chemicals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a facility- and emission-point-level listing of emitted HAPs and supporting data
rubrics_metrics.description: The record provides no listing of the individual HAPs emitted by each emission point at each facility, preventing public evaluation of how EPA calculated total emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must include these lists and supporting data/evidence of inventory completeness so the public can submit informed comments under CAA § 307.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use stack sampling and other direct measurements where feasible as preferred estimation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Stack sampling is the preferred emission estimation methodology for many pollutants (NOx, CO, VOC, THC, PM2.5/PM10, metals, speciated organics) absent cost considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to EIIP/Eastern Research Group guidance: collect samples via probes through stack ports and lab analysis; use measured data rather than model-only estimates when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA has authority to require data collection from states or industry under CAA §114
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA has full authority to request emission test data from states and to collect these data directly from industry facilities or require testing under CAA section 114, and it must do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statutory authorities proactively to obtain representative measured emissions data for the risk assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider hydrogen sulfide (H2S) exposures and listing under CAA §112
rubrics_metrics.description: Production/processing plants that handle 'sour gas' release significant H2S, which is toxic and not currently listed as a HAP under section 112, but EPA has a pending petition and has recognized H2S risks in other contexts (TRI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA has sufficient toxicity data to list/regulate H2S for oil and gas facilities and should act on the petition or otherwise address H2S in the residual risk assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate community health information and local/state health agency findings
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must collect, consider and address available information about community health impacts (CDC/ATSDR, AOEC, PEHSU, state health departments, local investigations) as part of the residual risk assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local investigations (e.g., ATSDR Garfield County) reported health complaints (dizziness, nausea, respiratory problems, eye/skin irritation, cancer concerns); EPA should analyze such data when assessing residual risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not omit fugitive and intermittent sources (drilling, completion, valves, etc.) because accumulated emissions can be significant
rubrics_metrics.description: Fugitive and intermittent sources (production equipment fugitives, well drilling, well completions, gas processing, transmission fugitives, pneumatic valves) can accumulate and constitute significant emissions; EPA must assess and regulate them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies indicate fugitive emissions may be a measurable fraction of production (e.g., Armendariz estimates); EPA should evaluate system-wide accumulation rather than ignoring many small sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: When prior MACT failed to set required limits, residual risk rule must compensate
rubrics_metrics.description: If EPA previously missed required MACT limits for uncontrolled emission points, then the residual risk rulemaking must do more to make up for the lack of health protection provided earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past failures to set MACT limits (e.g., 1999 omission) justify stricter residual risk-based standards now to ensure protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide reasoned explanations for any exclusions or decisions (avoid arbitrary and capricious reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must adequately explain its decisions not to assess or regulate certain emission points or HAPs; unexplained exclusions are arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any exclusion (e.g., of a valve type, emission point, chemical, metal) must be justified on the record with clear rationale and data support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess potential emissions from produced water, condensate tanks, and wastewater impoundments as potentially large HAP sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Produced water/condensate tanks and wastewater impoundments have been estimated to emit large amounts of HAPs (e.g., Colorado data showing >100 tpy VOCs from condensate tanks); EPA must investigate and consider regulating these sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include such storage/handling and loading operations in the emissions inventory and risk modelling; do not assume they are insignificant.
